It shows what's configured in .env and the redirect URI to register with the provider, and it lets you run a test login. The built-in admin login always keeps working as a fallback, so a broken SSO setup can't lock you out.

sections.Google sign-in: Status of the Sign in with Google button: on, half-configured (with the missing pieces listed), or not configured. Access is controlled by the GOOGLE_ADMIN_EMAILS, GOOGLE_OPERATOR_EMAILS and GOOGLE_VIEWER_EMAILS lists in .env. An email in more than one list gets the highest role, and any account not listed is refused. Google users skip Protek's TOTP, so turn on 2-Step Verification on those Google accounts. After you remove an email and restart Protek, that person is signed out on their next click.
sections.OpenID Connect SSO: Status of the generic OIDC login (Authentik, Auth0, Keycloak, Google and others), set with the OIDC_* variables in .env. Roles come from the user's groups claim (OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM, default groups) matched against OIDC_GROUPS_ADMIN, OIDC_GROUPS_OPERATOR and OIDC_GROUPS_VIEWER, optionally restricted to the email domains in OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS. Users matching no group are refused unless OIDC_DEFAULT_ROLE is set. Test login runs a real sign-in and shows the claims and the role Protek would assign, without signing you in as that user.

onboarding.intro: The setup guide is a first-run checklist with five steps: confirm Protek can reach the CrowdSec LAPI (CrowdSec's local API, where bans come from), add a bouncer target (a firewall such as your MikroTik that enforces the bans), switch a target from dry-run (simulate only) to live, optionally add more CrowdSec sources, and set up a notification channel. Steps are marked done automatically from Protek's real state, and operators can skip the ones they don't need. Once nothing is pending, Dismiss banner hides the setup reminder, and the page stays reachable afterwards.

admin_users.intro: Manage the local accounts that sign in to Protek with a username, password and authenticator (TOTP) code. Use it to give someone read-only or operator access, change a role, or turn an account off without deleting it. Admin only.

sections.New user created — capture TOTP NOW: Appears once, right after you create a user. It shows the username, role, the TOTP secret (the seed an authenticator app uses to generate 6-digit codes) and the provisioning URI. Paste the secret or the URI into the user's authenticator app now: there is no QR code here, and the secret is never shown again and cannot be recovered.
sections.Add user: Creates a new local account with a password and an auto-generated TOTP secret. Every local user has to enter an authenticator code at login, so give the person the secret from the box above straight away.
sections.Users: Every local account, with its role, when it was created, its last login, and whether it is active or disabled. User #1 (tagged "env") is the admin set up from the .env file: it is always admin and cannot be demoted, disabled or deleted. For other rows you can change the role, disable or enable the account, or delete it. People who sign in with Google aren't listed here. Their access comes from the GOOGLE_*_EMAILS lists in .env.

fields.username: Login name for the new account. Only letters, digits, underscores and hyphens are allowed; anything else is rejected.
fields.password: Initial password for the new account, at least 8 characters. Protek stores only a bcrypt hash of it, so give the password to the user through a separate channel.
fields.role: The account's permission level. In the Add user form it defaults to viewer. In the Users table, choosing a new value saves it straight away. viewer is read-only, operator can do everything except manage users and API tokens, and admin has full access.

admin_tokens.intro: Create and manage API tokens for scripts and tools that call Protek's /api/v1 endpoints without a browser login. Use it to give a CLI, a monitoring job or a public stats page its own credential that you can revoke. Admin only.

sections.New token — capture NOW: Shown once, right after you create a token. Copy the full token (it starts with pk_) now: Protek stores only a SHA-256 hash of it and cannot show it again. Send it as an "Authorization: Bearer <token>" header (an X-Protek-Token header also works).
sections.Create token: Makes a new token with a name, one or more scopes and an optional expiry date. Scopes decide what the token may call: stats is the counts-only stats endpoint, read is all GET endpoints, write adds posting bans, sync and whitelist changes, and admin is everything.
sections.Tokens: Every token, with its first few characters (prefix) so you can identify it, its scopes, who created it, when it was last used and from which IP, its expiry, and its state. Revoke switches a token off but keeps the row for the record; delete removes it completely. "never" under Last used means the token has not been used yet. State only shows revoked or active, so an expired token still reads active even though Protek refuses it.

fields.name: A label so you can tell which tool owns the token, such as protekctl-laptop. Only letters, digits, underscores and hyphens are allowed.
fields.scopes: Comma-separated permissions, default read. Valid values are stats, read, write and admin. Higher scopes include the lower ones (admin > write > read > stats), but stats grants nothing else. Give each tool the smallest scope it needs.
fields.expires_at: Optional expiry as an ISO date-time, for example 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z. Leave it blank for a token that never expires; after the date passes, the token is refused. The date isn't checked when you create the token, and Protek ignores a value it can't parse, so a typo leaves the token with no expiry.

admin_backup.intro: Export Protek's configuration as a single passphrase-encrypted file, or restore it from one. Use it before rebuilding a server, when moving Protek to a new host, or to merge one instance's settings into another. It covers configuration only, not ban or alert history. For automatic full-database backups, use Backup (off-box).

sections.Export config bundle: Downloads an encrypted .bin file containing users, federation sources, the whitelist, router (bouncer) targets, webhook subscribers, API token hashes, all settings including notification credentials, and alert silences. It leaves out decisions, alerts, sync history and the audit log, because Protek rebuilds that data from CrowdSec. Nobody can open the file without the passphrase.
sections.Import config bundle: Restores a bundle created by the export above. Additive mode (the default) keeps every existing row and adds only the rows that are missing. Overwrite mode empties each table in the bundle and replaces its contents from the bundle, which suits a fresh server.
sections.Last import: Appears once, after an import. For each table it shows how many rows were in the bundle and how many were inserted, replaced or skipped, so you can check that the restore did what you expected. In additive mode rows that already existed count as skipped; in overwrite mode restored rows count as replaced.

fields.passphrase: On export, the passphrase that encrypts the bundle. It must be at least 12 characters, and if you lose it the bundle cannot be opened. On import, enter the passphrase that was used for the export. A wrong one fails with a decryption error and changes nothing.
fields.file: The .bin bundle file to restore, created by Export config bundle on this Protek instance or another one.
fields.overwrite: Unticked by default (additive: existing rows are kept). Tick it to wipe each table in the bundle and replace its contents, for example when restoring onto a fresh install. Any rows on this instance that aren't in the bundle are lost, including users and API tokens.

admin_backup_auto.intro: Set up and monitor automatic encrypted backups of Protek's full database, its .env file and any custom CrowdSec scenarios, kept on local disk or in S3-compatible storage. Use it to make sure you could rebuild after losing the server, and to confirm the backups actually restore. This is separate from Backup (config), which is a manual export of configuration only.

sections.BACKUP_PASSPHRASE missing: Appears only when BACKUP_PASSPHRASE is not set in .env. Every backup fails until you add a long random passphrase there and restart Protek. Keep a copy somewhere safe, because the backups can't be decrypted without it.
sections.Configuration: How backups are scheduled, where they're kept and how many are kept. On a server with the nightly timer installed, leave the built-in schedule off, or backups run twice. Backend local keeps them on this server (and copies them off-box when a bucket is set up below); s3 only keeps them only in the bucket.
sections.Litestream WAL replication: Optional, and most installs don't need it: the nightly backup and its off-box copy already cover a lost server. Litestream streams every database change to a bucket as it happens, so you'd lose at most about a minute instead of up to a day — at the cost of constant disk and memory use. Shown in the advanced view, or whenever it's installed. The badge says whether it's running, lagging or not installed; follow the install steps one at a time.
sections.Manual actions: Run backup now takes a full backup immediately, outside the schedule. Run restore-test now downloads the newest backup, decrypts it in a temporary folder and runs a database integrity check without touching the live database.
sections.Recent runs: The last 30 backup and restore-test runs, with kind (manual, daily, monthly or test), status, size, backend and destination. For a failed run the destination column shows the error, and hovering over FAILED shows it as well.
sections.Off-box copy (Backblaze B2): Sends a copy of every verified backup to a storage bucket off this server — Backblaze B2, AWS S3 or MinIO — so losing the server doesn't lose its backups. The file is already encrypted before it leaves. Test and save uploads, reads back and deletes a small test file first, so a wrong key or bucket is caught straight away. Local backups carry on either way.
sections.Backup status: A summary of your backups: what schedules them, where they're stored, whether the encryption passphrase is set, the last good backup, the off-box copy and the last restore test. If Schedule, Off-box copy and Restore-test are green, backups are working.

kpis.Passphrase: Whether BACKUP_PASSPHRASE is set in .env. SET is what you need; MISSING means every backup fails.
kpis.Last successful: Time, size and kind of the most recent good backup, counting manual ones. With a nightly schedule, it should be no more than about a day old. A dash means no backup has succeeded yet.
kpis.Restore-test: Result of the last check that the newest backup decrypts and passes an integrity check. OK is what you want. FAIL means the backups may not be restorable and needs attention now. A dash means no test has succeeded yet; failures are only marked FAIL after at least one earlier test has passed. The time underneath is the last test that passed.
kpis.Off-box copy: Whether the last backup was also copied to your off-box bucket. OK shows when and how big; FAILING means the last upload didn't work (the local backup is still fine) and the reason is shown below; OFF means no bucket is set up yet.
kpis.Schedule: What runs the backups. NIGHTLY means the server's own nightly timer (protek-backup.timer) is doing it — the usual setup. BUILT-IN means Protek's own scheduler is on. OFF means there's been no backup in the last 36 hours, so nothing is running them: install the timer or turn on the built-in schedule.
kpis.Stored on: Where backups are kept. THIS SERVER means a folder here (/var/backups/protek by default), with an off-box copy too once a bucket is set up. BUCKET ONLY means they go straight to the bucket with no copy here. Red means the storage can't be reached, with the reason underneath.

fields.enabled: Turns on Protek's own scheduler: a daily backup, a monthly one, and a weekly restore test. Only for servers without the nightly system timer — with both, every backup runs twice.
fields.backend: Where to keep backups. On this server is the usual choice: backups go to the folder below, and to the off-box bucket too once one is set up. Only in the bucket skips the copy here — only pick it if this server has no room.
fields.local_path: The folder on this server where backups are kept. /var/backups/protek by default.
fields.daily_keep: How many daily backups to keep before the oldest are deleted, default 30 (allowed range 1–365).
fields.monthly_keep: How many monthly backups to keep, default 12 (allowed range 1–120). Monthly backups give you older restore points after the daily ones have been deleted.
fields.s3_endpoint: The bucket's S3 endpoint. For Backblaze it's on the bucket's page, e.g. https://s3.us-west-002.backblazeb2.com. Leave it blank for AWS S3.
fields.s3_region: The bucket's region, e.g. us-west-002. Left blank with a Backblaze endpoint, it's read from the endpoint; for AWS use the bucket's region, like eu-central-1.
fields.s3_bucket: The name of the bucket to copy backups into. A bucket used only for Protek is simplest; backups go under daily/ and monthly/ and keep the same retention as here.
fields.s3_key: The key ID of an access key for that bucket — in Backblaze, the keyID of an application key limited to this bucket with Read and Write access.
fields.s3_secret: The secret that goes with the key ID (Backblaze: the applicationKey, shown once when you create it). Stored in .env and never shown again; leave it blank to keep the current one.

dr_drill.intro: Record a disaster-recovery practice run: work through the recovery checklist, run the automated checks, and log what passed. Do it about once a quarter, so you find broken backups or notifications before you need them. Each recorded drill goes into the audit log, which can only be added to, never edited.

sections.Quarterly disaster-recovery drill: The checklist from docs/DR-RUNBOOK.md. Four checks have a Run button that tests the live system and ticks the box if the check passes (or unticks it if it fails): restore-test, synthetic ban test, Litestream restore, and notifications. Two checks are manual: restoring onto a scratch server, and re-pushing to a replacement MikroTik. Tick those yourself once you have done them. Record drill saves the ticks and your notes.
sections.Drill history (tamper-evident audit log): The last 12 recorded drills, with the date, who ran each one, how many of the 6 checks passed, and the start of the saved details (which boxes were ticked, plus your notes). Use it to show that drills happen regularly and to spot checks that keep failing.

fields.restore_to_scratch: Tick this after you have restored the latest backup onto a scratch server by hand, aiming for under 30 minutes (runbook sections 1 and 6). There is no Run button; this check is manual only.
fields.restore_test_ok: Run is meant to re-run the backup restore-test and tick the box on success, but in this build it always reports "restore-test crashed". Instead, use Run restore-test now on the Backup (off-box) page, and tick this box by hand if that passes.
fields.synthetic_passed: Run pushes a test ban for 192.0.2.250 (a documentation-only address) directly to each enabled, non-dry-run router, checks that it appears in the router's address list, then removes it and checks that it's gone. The box ticks only if every router passes. If every router is in dry-run (log-only) mode, the test is skipped and counts as a fail.
fields.litestream_restore: Run restores the Litestream replica into a temporary file in RAM (/dev/shm), checks the result, then deletes the file, without touching the live database. It fails if the restore script or Litestream isn't installed. It can take up to 10 minutes before timing out.
fields.notifications_tested: Run sends a test message to each configured channel (Discord, Telegram, email). It passes only if at least one channel is configured and none of them fail. Check that the messages actually arrived.
fields.mt_replacement: Tick this after you have checked by hand that a replacement or factory-reset MikroTik gets the full ban list pushed back to it from scratch. It is a physical, manual-only check.
fields.note: Optional free-text notes saved with the drill in the audit log, up to 500 characters (longer text is cut off), such as what surprised you or what to fix in the runbook.

admin_ha.intro: Shows whether this Protek host is the primary (the one actively pushing bans to MikroTik) or a standby copy, and lets you hand that role over manually. It only matters if you run two Protek servers with Litestream copying the database between them. On a single server it just reads PRIMARY and you can ignore it. Admin only.

sections.Active-passive HA: Shows this host's current role and its heartbeat, which is how many seconds have passed since the sync loop last finished a cycle. On the primary, the heartbeat should stay under the stale threshold (60 seconds by default, adjustable with the ha.heartbeat_stale_sec setting); above that it turns red and shows STALE. On a standby the heartbeat comes from the replicated database, so a growing number means the primary has stopped. The role comes from the ha.role setting first, then the HA_ROLE env var, and defaults to primary if neither is set. Underneath is the last role change, who made it and why.
sections.Promote to primary: Shown on a standby. Makes this host the primary. After you restart Protek it runs the sync loop and owns writes to MikroTik. Only do this when the old primary is really down, or both servers will push to the router.
sections.Demote to standby: Shown on the primary. Makes this host a standby, so after a restart it stops syncing to MikroTik. Promote the other host first, or nothing will be syncing bans.
sections.Manual failover runbook: Steps for a manual failover: confirm the primary is down, stop Litestream on the standby, promote the standby, restart Protek, update DNS if needed, then demote the old primary when it comes back. Failover is never automatic, because without a proper consensus system a network split could leave two primaries fighting over the router.

fields.confirm: Type this server's exact hostname to confirm the promote or demote. If it doesn't match, nothing changes. This stops you from switching the wrong server by mistake.
fields.reason: Optional note saved in the audit log with the role change (up to 300 characters), such as "primary outage; cut over to standby". If you leave it blank, "manual promote via /admin/ha" or "manual demote via /admin/ha" is recorded instead.

crowdsec.intro: A read-only view of CrowdSec's local API (the LAPI), which hands out ban decisions to bouncers such as Protek. Use it to check that CrowdSec is reachable, and to see its raw data when a ban isn't showing up as expected. Protek adds its bouncer key on the server, so your browser never sees the key.

sections.LAPI Endpoints (auth-proxied through Pro: Links to common LAPI queries. Each one opens the raw JSON response in a new tab, through your Protek login. Endpoints marked bouncer work with Protek's key. Endpoints marked machine (alerts, bouncers, machines) need agent credentials and normally return 401, which is expected. Only read-only GET requests are allowed; make changes with cscli on the server.
sections.Quick Peek — Active Decisions: The first 10 active IP ban decisions as raw JSON, straight from the LAPI. Each entry shows the IP, scenario, duration and origin. An empty [] means no IP bans are active. If the LAPI can't be reached, a message appears here instead.
sections.cscli commands (run on VPS shell): A reference list of CrowdSec command-line commands to run on the server. They cover listing and inspecting bans and alerts, listing bouncers and machines, viewing metrics, adding or removing a ban by hand, and managing the hub and console.

kpis.LAPI Endpoint: The LAPI address Protek is set up to use, and whether it answered a check just now. It should read reachable. Unreachable means CrowdSec is down, the URL is wrong, or the bouncer key is missing or rejected; while it stays that way, no new bans reach the router.
kpis.Active Decisions: How many active IP ban decisions the LAPI returns to Protek's bouncer key right now. Range (CIDR) bans aren't counted here. Zero is normal on a quiet system, but a sudden drop to zero while CrowdSec is running is worth checking.
kpis.Bouncers: This doesn't query CrowdSec: it shows 1 (Protek itself), or 0 if no bouncer key is configured. Run "cscli bouncers list" for the real list. The note underneath always reads "bouncer key only".
kpis.Prometheus: Where CrowdSec's own metrics are served on this server (127.0.0.1:6060/metrics). The address is fixed text, only reachable from the server itself, and no live value is shown.
